newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan indicted oil monopoly head sacked. [CORRECTED 10:37 GMT 24/12]
newsitem.headline: Taiwan indicted oil monopoly head sacked. [CORRECTED 10:37 GMT 24/12]

text.p: Chang Tzu-yuan, chairman of state-owned Chinese Petroleum Corp, was replaced on Tuesday after being indicted on charges unrelated to his duties at Taiwan's oil monopoly.
Chang was replaced by Lee Shu-jeou (corrects name), a vice minister at the economics ministry that oversees the state-owned company, ministry officials said at a news conference.
"Chang Tzu-yuan has been transferred to be an adviser to the ministry," vice minister Chang Chang-pang, also from the economics ministry, said.
"The reason he is being replaced is that he will face a lot of legal proceedings," Chang said.

Chang Tzu-yuan was charged in connection to land-zoning improprieties allegedly committed during his tenure as mayor of Taiwan's central Taichung city several years ago, officials said. He faces up to six years in prison if convicted.
Chang Tzu-yuan has proclaimed his innocence.

His indictment was the latest in a string of blows to Taiwan's oil giant, where president Chen Kuo-young resigned on November 19 to take responsibility for a series of explosions, fires and oil spills that cost the company millions of dollars in compensation claims and fines in 1996.

Chinese Petroleum, which reported a huge budget deficit in November, finally saw its fiscal 1996-97 budget adopted by parliament last Thursday after months of political footdragging over its proposed privatisation and other contentious issues.

The budget stalemate and popular opposition have prevented Chinese Petroleum from carrying through oil price increases that would enable it to balance its budget at a time when world oil prices are sharply higher that it had anticipated.

Parliament cut the monopoly's budget for key overseas expansion programmes in Indonesia and Vietnam and cancelled its participation in a consortium planning to build a power station in northern Taiwan.
Before his indictment, Chang Tzu-yuan had vowed to stay on at Chinese Petroleum despite mounting criticism of his stewardship from lawmakers, government officials and Taiwan's media.
